tasks.short: Watch behaviour patterns, note triggers, agree an approach with parents, write it down and apply it every day.

steps.what: Nanny watches the child's behaviour patterns over several days
Nanny notes incidents and triggers: on paper today, in the family profile after the change
Nanny works with parents to agree a discipline approach
Nanny writes the agreed rules and rewards: on a sheet today, in the family profile after the change
Nanny applies the approach consistently to promote desirable behavior
Parents apply the same approach in evenings and weekends

tasks.design: Nothing changes in this task's time. The nanny may keep incident notes and the agreed rules and rewards in the family profile of the agency's parent app ({OTHER}) instead of on loose paper, but writing them takes the same time, and the nanny still goes through the notes with the parents in their talk. Watching, agreeing and applying the approach stay with nanny and parents.
tasks.previous_blocker: Notes and agreements lived on loose paper.
tasks.enabler_now: Dutch parent apps hold a daily diary and family information.
tasks.still_hard: Behaviour notes about a child need tact and should stay between nanny and parents.
tasks.human_edge: Staying consistent and warm with a child who is testing limits.

reach.learn: Whether shared patterns help parents and staff agree.

evidence.claim: A Dutch parent app gives parents a daily report in a digital diary.
Notes about a child's behaviour are personal data to share only with the parents.

assumptions: Boundary: from noticing patterns to applying the approach; professional help is outside.
Input contract: diary and family profile set up by the agency with parents' consent; fallback is paper.
Parent time is outside the nanny's savings.
Scenario: the nanny works through an agency with a parent app.

Noting incidents and writing the agreed rules are first records by the nanny and keep their full time; typing them instead of writing saves nothing. Saving them in the family profile is the nanny's own record and needs no approval.
unknowns: Whether the parents read the diary daily.
research_questions: Do shared notes make nanny and parents more consistent?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: the agency sets up the family profile, and learning its fields is a one-off.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: No saving: watching, agreeing and applying stay in person, and the notes and rules are first records that take as long in the app as on paper (0.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Gather the week's events, meet parents about activities and development, plan next week and note agreements.

steps.what: Nanny gathers the week's events from memory and notes
Nanny meets regularly with parents to discuss activities and development
Parents enter their fixed appointments for next week (school, clubs, visits) in the shared family calendar
Nanny and parents plan next week's schedule: by chat today, in the shared family calendar after the change
Nanny writes down what was agreed: on paper today, in the family profile after the change

tasks.design: A week summary is built from the day reports in the agency's parent app ({OTHER}) for the nanny to check before the talk, the parents enter their fixed appointments in a shared family {CALENDAR} where nanny and parents plan next week, and the nanny writes the agreements in the family profile. The talk with the parents stays as it is.
tasks.previous_blocker: The week was recalled from memory, and schedules were agreed in long chat threads.
tasks.enabler_now: Parent apps keep day reports, and shared calendars are standard.
tasks.still_hard: Talking about a child's development needs trust and care.
tasks.human_edge: Telling parents honestly what their child is like when they are not there.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes; the talk starts from a summary.

reach.task: Check in with families and nannies
reach.learn: Whether week summaries show where families need support.

evidence.claim: A Dutch parent app shows parents a timeline, daily report and agenda.

assumptions: Boundary: from preparing the talk to notes made; development concerns referred elsewhere are outside.
Input contract: day reports entered by the nanny; shared calendar set up by the parents; fallback is memory and chat.
Parent time, including entering their appointments (s3p, share 1), is outside the nanny's savings.

The talk and writing down the agreements keep their full time. s1 keeps 40 because the nanny still checks the summary and adds what the day reports miss. s3 keeps 80 because the parents' fixed appointments are already in the calendar, so the nanny no longer asks for them by chat; the week is still agreed with the parents.
unknowns: How often the nanny and parents meet.
research_questions: Do summaries change what nanny and parents talk about?

already_counted.description: Nanny checks the generated week summary.

incremental.description: Nanny keeps the shared calendar current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the day reports miss about half the week's events and the parents do not keep the calendar, so planning stays in chat (5.7); high: the summary covers most of the week and the parents keep the calendar (11.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check the planner, supervise homework, look up how the school explains a method, explain it and tell the parents.

steps.what: Nanny checks the child's planner for today's homework
Nanny sits with the child and supervises homework
Nanny searches how the school teaches a method the child is stuck on

loop.input: The exercise text (no child data) and the name of the school's maths or reading method.
loop.output: A step-by-step explanation in that method's terms with one similar practice example.
loop.check: For sums the final answer is recomputed by a calculator and must match; the steps must use the method's named strategy; the nanny reads the explanation before using it and drops it if it differs from the child's book.
loop.stop: One answer per question; if the check fails the nanny asks the parents or the teacher.
loop.why_not_simpler: Schools teach the same sum in different ways; a calculator gives only the answer, not the method.

steps.what: Nanny assists the child with explanations of what they do not understand
Nanny writes the parents what was done and what was hard: in a chat today, in the day report after the change
Nanny reads the final update: it says what was done and what was hard as it went, and it goes to this child's parents
Nanny sends the checked homework update to the parents

tasks.design: When the child is stuck, the nanny asks a bounded explainer for the school method's steps on that exercise, with sums rechecked by a calculator, and reads it before helping. Homework done is a tick in the day report of the agency's parent app ({OTHER}) and the nanny still writes what was hard, reads the update and sends it; supervising and explaining stay with the nanny.
tasks.previous_blocker: Nannies searched videos or guessed how the school taught a method.
tasks.enabler_now: Language models explain exercises step by step, and a calculator can check the answer.
tasks.still_hard: Explanations can differ from the school's way; the tool must never do the child's homework or judge the child.
tasks.human_edge: Keeping a tired child going and knowing when to stop.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes; the nanny explains with more confidence.

evidence.claim: AI that evaluates learning outcomes is high-risk; an explainer used by the nanny does not evaluate the child.
Language models can explain exercises step by step when answers are rechecked.
A Dutch parent app gives parents a daily report.

assumptions: Boundary: from checking the planner to telling parents; tutoring by the school is outside.
Input contract: method names given by parents from the school's information; exercise text typed by the nanny without the child's name; fallback is asking parents.

Checking the planner, supervising, explaining, reading and sending the update keep their full time. s3 keeps 50 because the nanny still types the exercise, reads the explanation and compares it with the child's book. s5 keeps 85 because only the done mark becomes a tick; what was hard is still written by the nanny.
The explainer is used by the nanny, not by the child.
unknowns: How often the child gets stuck on methods.
research_questions: Do method-specific explanations match what teachers expect?

already_counted.description: Nanny reads each explanation before using it.

incremental.description: Nanny keeps the school method names at hand.

approvals.approved_version: The homework update exactly as read by the nanny in s5c, sent once to this child's parents in the parent app; any change needs a new read.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the explanation often differs from the child's book so the nanny still searches, and the parents keep the chat (1.7); high: explanations match the school method and the day report is used (5.9).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Record play and meals, plan meals, record hours, get parents to confirm, get paid through the agency and claim grocery costs.

steps.what: Nanny records play and meals: in a paper notebook today, in quick fields of the day report after the change
Nanny plans meal schedules for the week with the parents: on paper today, in the family profile after the change, where last week's plan is carried over
Nanny records the hours worked each day: on a paper timesheet today, in the app after the change, which totals the month
Parents check the month's hours against the days the nanny worked and confirm them: by signing paper today, in the app after the change
The confirmed hours go to the agency for invoicing: today the nanny sends them and chases payment
Nanny keeps grocery receipts and totals them: in an envelope today, by photographing each receipt and typing its amount in the app after the change
Nanny checks the month's grocery claim: each receipt is for this family's groceries and each amount matches its photo
Nanny submits the checked grocery claim to the parents for repayment
Agency administrator retypes hours, invoices the parents and pays the nanny

tasks.design: Play and meals are recorded in quick fields of the day report in the agency's parent app ({OTHER}) instead of a notebook, the meal plan sits in the family profile, and the nanny enters hours per day in the same app, which totals them. Parents check and confirm the month's hours there; the confirmed hours go to the agency, which invoices the parents and pays the nanny by bank. The nanny photographs grocery receipts into the app, checks the month's claim and submits it to the parents for repayment.
tasks.previous_blocker: Notebooks, paper timesheets and e-mailed hours were retyped by the agency.
tasks.enabler_now: Dutch parent apps hold day reports, and agencies collect and pass on payments by bank as childcare allowance rules require.
tasks.still_hard: Parents must confirm on time; some prefer paper.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing what each child ate and played and telling it with care.
tasks.altitude: The nanny records once; billing is the agency's and the parents' confirmation, not the nanny's chasing.

reach.learn: Whether confirmed hours end retyping and disputes.

evidence.claim: A Dutch parent app gives parents a timeline, daily report and agenda.
Home childcare costs go through the agency, which collects and passes on payments by bank, not cash.

assumptions: Boundary: from daily records to the nanny paid and groceries repaid; tax filing is outside.
Input contract: hourly rates and family accounts kept by the agency; hours entered by the nanny and confirmed by parents in the app; fallback is paper timesheets.
Parent and agency time is outside the nanny's savings.
Scenario: the nanny works through an agency, as needed for childcare allowance.

Recording play and meals is a first record and keeps its full time. s2 keeps 90 because only rewriting recurring meals goes. s3 keeps 85 because the nanny still enters each day's hours; the app only totals them. s5 is gone because the agency invoices and collects. s6 keeps 60 because the nanny still photographs each receipt and types its amount; sorting and totalling go. Checking and submitting the claim keep their full time.
unknowns: Whether the agency's app takes hours entry.
research_questions: Does in-app confirmation shorten time to payment?

already_counted.description: Nanny corrects hours that parents query.

incremental.description: Agency keeps rates and family accounts current.
No ongoing focal upkeep: the agency keeps rates and accounts, learning the screens is a one-off, and correcting queried hours is counted in s3.

approvals.approved_version: The month's hours per day exactly as checked and confirmed by the parents in s4, passed once to the agency for invoicing the parents and paying the nanny; any correction needs a new confirmation.
The month's grocery claim with each receipt photo and amount exactly as checked by the nanny in s6c, submitted once to this family's parents in the app for repayment; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: parents confirm late, so the nanny still chases about a third of the months, and receipts stay on paper (16.7); high: hours confirmed and receipts claimed in the app (28.1).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The nanny keeps the children's day and the talks with parents; notebooks, timesheets and payment chasing move to the agency app.
skills_to_grow: Recording the day briefly in the app
role.ambitious_version: A nanny who is paid on time without chasing and spends every working hour with the children.
